## **The Holy Family from Outer Space: reconsidering philip K. Dick’s** _**The Divine Invasion**_ 

## **umbErto roSSi** 

■ In Roger Luckhurst’s _Science Fiction_ (2005), we can find this trenchant assessment of Philip Kindred Dick’s oeuvre: 

Although Dick wrote a number of novels within [. . .] Realist conventions, he perceived himself as a genre writer [. . .] To lift two or three Dick novels into the ‘literate’ New Wave or into a separate tradition of SF-as-critical-theory is to canonize by isolating those works from the confusing and confused avalanche of SF he produced in the 1960s. The later phases of Dick’s career deepened the resonances with structures of technological paranoia [. . .] but Dick’s vision remained absolutely continuous with the satirical and psychological fictions typically associated with the works of Pohl, Kornbluth and Sheckley in the 1950s. Dick did not substantially depart from that tradition. (163) 

Since the other three writers mentioned by Luckhurst belong to the current of sociological science-fiction, which the British critic brilliantly and exhaustively describes in another part of his history of the genre (109-19), one cannot agree _in toto_ .[1] Dick did begin as an author of sociological sf, but he moved to very different territories after 1960—the moment of the departure arguably being marked by the publication of _The Man in the High Castle_ (1962), as it is an alternate history (not found in sociological sf) or by _Martian Time-Slip_ (1964), due to the sophistication of its narrative structure and the central theme of schizophrenia.[2]

## UMBERTO ROSSI 

Yet Luckhurst’s assessment might be reinterpreted in such a way that suggests a productive reading of one of Dick’s less discussed novels, the second part of the VALIS Trilogy, _The Divine Invasion_ (1981). Though Dick did depart from sociological sf, he never lost sight of the sociological aspects of sf—he never forgot he belonged to U.S. society, and always managed to offer us surprising and original insights about it in a crucial phase of its history (from the end of World War Two to the election of Ronald Reagan). 

Such sociological awareness can also be found in _The Divine Invasion_ , a novel where we do not just find the typical devices of sf (e.g. space travel, colonization of other planets, hibernation, world government) but also supernatural entities from the Old Testament (Yah—that is the Jewish God—his adversary Belial, the prophet Elijah, etc.), plus borrowings from Gnosticism and the Jewish Kabbalah, not to mention such a traditional Christian image as the Holy Family. And it is this famous family which will guide us in our reading, inasmuch as it is a religious symbol, celebrated every year on Christmas Day, but—being a family—it is also a social entity, one of the bricks on which any human society is based.
